topic: HTTP Keep-Alive Silently Breaks Canary Traffic Splitting
postText:
You configure a 2% canary release for a critical clinical ingestion service at 02:00 AM. Five minutes later, telemetry reports that canary instance taking 40% of all write volume, starving its downstream connection pool.

What happened? Layer 4 persistent connection reuse.

Modern clients, service meshes, and ingress proxies use persistent HTTP/2 or HTTP Keep-Alive connections. When upstream balancers route at connection establishment instead of per-request L7 frame level, high-throughput batch clients lock onto single canary workers for entire operational lifecycles.

In our healthcare IT environments, medical equipment interfaces hold TCP sockets open for days. Routing percentages fail completely when load distribution presumes stateless, short-lived sockets.

To achieve true zero-downtime canary validation under persistent connections:
1. Enforce strict L7 stream-aware proxy dispatching (Envoy, HAProxy) over simple TCP round-robin.
2. Inject proactive Keep-Alive max request thresholds (`keepalive_requests` in Nginx or upstream max stream limits in Envoy) to force re-evaluation of target weights.
3. Bound canary database connection pools strictly to traffic weight proportions to prevent accidental resource exhaustion on backend clusters.

Real zero-downtime releases require visibility all the way down to TCP socket lifetimes.

How do your ingress topologies enforce strict canary percentages when clients maintain long-lived HTTP/2 streams or persistent TCP sockets?
